power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Health workforce shortages in sub-Saharan Africa are compounded by how existing staff are managed, yet little quantitative evidence describes how hospital health professionals in Ethiopia perceive human resource management (HRM) practices or which workplace conditions accompany those perceptions.

Drawing on social exchange theory, we assessed health professionals' perceptions of HRM practices and their associations with workplace "cost" factors (job demands) and "benefit" factors (job resources) in public hospitals of Gamo Zone, southern Ethiopia.
We conducted an institution-based cross-sectional survey from 15 February to 15 March 2025 in three of the zone's six public hospitals, selected by lottery.
Randomly sampled health professionals completed a structured questionnaire on tablets.

Perception of HRM practices was measured with 28 five-point items covering seven practice domains and summarized as a mean score from 1 to 5; a mean above 3.0 was classified as a favorable perception.
Associations were estimated with multivariable linear regression using heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors, adjusting for age, sex, profession and hospital.
After removal of 41 duplicate records and 52 ineligible non-health staff, 343 health professionals were analyzed.
The mean HRM perception score was 2.81 (standard deviation 0.58), and 29.0% (99/341; 95% confidence interval [CI] 24.5-34.1%) of participants held a favorable perception.
Recruitment and training and development were rated least favorably, and selection most favorably.
The proportion with a favorable perception ranged from 1.5% at the general hospital to 55.5% at one primary hospital.

In the adjusted model (n = 326; R² = 0.46), greater perceived autonomy (β = 0.20 per scale point; 95% CI 0.06 to 0.35) and recognition (β = 0.12; 95% CI 0.02 to 0.22) were independently associated with more favorable perceptions.

Skill ambiguity, work-life role conflict, schedule variability and interpersonal conflict were associated with less favorable perceptions in unadjusted analyses, but no cost factor remained independently associated after adjustment (joint test p = 0.459).
Fewer than one in three health professionals viewed HRM practices favorably, with large differences between hospitals.
Perceived recognition and autonomy, rather than job demands, were the workplace factors most consistently associated with how staff appraised HRM.
These findings point to hospital-level management and non-financial job resources as priorities for health workforce governance research and practice in comparable low-resource settings.
An adequate, motivated and well-managed health workforce is a precondition for universal health coverage.

The World Health Organization's Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health: Workforce 2030 projected a global shortfall of 18 million health workers [1]; a later reassessment revised this to about 10 million by 2030, with the shortage increasingly concentrated in the WHO African Region [2].

text.text: Shortages, however, are only part of the problem.

Systematic reviews from low-and middle-income countries consistently identify career development, continuing education, management practices and recognition, alongside pay, as central to health worker motivation and retention [4, 5].

text.text: How HRM affects staff depends not only on formal policies but on how employees experience and interpret them.

Research on HR attributions and HRM system strength shows that the same practice can elicit different attitudes depending on whether employees perceive it as fair, consistent and intended to support them [8, 9].

text.text: Yet health professionals' perceptions of HRM practices themselves have rarely been measured.

The only Ethiopian study we identified, an unpublished master's thesis from Metekel Zone (n = 211), reported that 55% of health professionals perceived HRM practices as good and that poor training, workforce planning and performance appraisal were associated with poor perceptions [16].

text.text: Social exchange theory offers a useful lens for examining these perceptions.
It views employment as a reciprocal exchange in which employees weigh what they invest against what they receive from the organization [18, 19].

text.text: Organizational support theory, which builds on it, shows that favorable treatment-such as recognition and discretion over one's workstrengthens employees' beliefs that the organization values them, whereas unfavorable treatment erodes them [20] [21] [22].

text.text: Following this logic, we grouped workplace conditions into "cost" factors (workload, skill ambiguity, work-life role conflict, organizational constraints, work schedule variability and interpersonal conflict) and "benefit" factors (social support, recognition and autonomy).

Whether demands or resources are more closely tied to how health professionals appraise HRM in low-resource hospitals is not known, and the answer matters for management: resources such as recognition and autonomy may be more amenable to hospital-level action than workload, which is driven largely by staffing.

This study therefore aimed (i) to describe health professionals' perceptions of HRM practices in public hospitals of Gamo Zone, southern Ethiopia, overall, by practice domain and by hospital, and (ii) to examine the associations of workplace cost and benefit factors with these perceptions, independent of individual characteristics and hospital.
Both aims were addressed after an audit of the study dataset that identified and removed duplicate and ineligible records.
We conducted an institution-based cross-sectional study and report it according to the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guideline [24] (S1 Checklist).

text.text: Gamo Zone lies in South Ethiopia Regional State; its administrative center, Arba Minch, is about 505 km south of Addis Ababa.

According to the Gamo Zone Health Department, the zone had six public hospitals-Arba Minch General Hospital and five primary hospitals (Dilfana, Selamber, Chencha, Kamba and Gerese)-employing about 990 health professionals, excluding administrative staff, of whom 412 worked at Arba Minch General Hospital.
Data were collected from 15 February to 15 March 2025.
The source population was all health professionals employed in public hospitals of Gamo Zone.

Health professionals were defined as staff with clinical or allied health professional training (physicians, health officers, nurses, midwives, pharmacy, medical laboratory, health informatics, radiology, anesthesia, environmental and public health professionals, and integrated emergency surgical officers).
Health professionals who had worked in a selected hospital for at least six months were eligible.
Those holding administrative or leadership positions (for example, hospital directors and unit heads) were excluded because they are responsible for implementing the practices being rated.
Non-health support and administrative staff were not part of the study population.

The sample size was calculated with the single population proportion formula, assuming that 55% of health professionals perceive HRM practices favorably [16], a 95% confidence level and a 5.1% margin of error (n = 366).

text.text: Items were rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
The overall perception score was the mean of the 28 items (range 1-5), and domain scores were the means of their four items.

text.text: Cost factors were workload (4 items), skill ambiguity (3 items), work-life role conflict (3 items), organizational constraints (5 items), work schedule variability (2 items) and interpersonal conflict (3 items).
Benefit factors were social support (4 items), recognition (3 items) and autonomy (6 items).
The role conflict items asked about conflict between job demands and responsibilities outside work, so we label this construct work-life role conflict.

All items used the same five-point agreement scale and were scored so that higher values indicate more of the named construct (greater demand for cost factors, greater resource for benefit factors); scale scores were item means (range 1-5).
The original thesis reverse-coded cost items; this changes the sign but not the magnitude of their coefficients.
Covariates were age (years), sex, profession and hospital.

Profession was grouped as nurse, midwife, health officer, physician (general practitioner or specialist) and other health professional; the last group comprised pharmacy, medical laboratory, health informatics (health information technicians, health statistics and medical records officers), public health, health extension, environmental health, radiology, anesthesia, integrated emergency surgery and infection prevention professionals ( S1 Table).

text.text: Excluding influential observations strengthened the associations of social support, skill ambiguity and interpersonal conflict, so the null findings for individual cost factors should be regarded as imprecise rather than as evidence of no association.
Replicating the original thesis approach of bivariable screening and backward elimination retained hospital, interpersonal conflict, recognition and autonomy.

In logistic regression of favorable perception, the odds ratios for autonomy (1.84; 95% CI 0.95-3.54) and recognition (1.56; 95% CI 0.98-2.49) were in the same direction but imprecise, as expected after dichotomizing the outcome.
There was weak evidence that the association with recognition differed by hospital (interaction p = 0.073).

In this survey of health professionals in three public hospitals in southern Ethiopia, fewer than one in three held a favorable view of HRM practices, and perceptions of recruitment and of training and development were particularly negative.
Perceptions varied more between hospitals than across any individual characteristic.

Among workplace factors, recognition and autonomy-two job resources-were independently associated with more favorable perceptions, whereas job demands such as workload, skill ambiguity and work-life role conflict, although high, were not independently associated once resources and hospital were taken into account.
The proportion with a favorable perception (29.0%) was lower than the 55% reported in Metekel Zone [16].
text.formatted: The proportion with a favorable perception (29.0%) was lower than the 55% reported in Metekel Zone <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[16]</ref>.

text.text: The domain pattern is more informative and is consistent with prior Ethiopian evidence.

In Metekel, poor training and development, workforce planning and performance appraisal were associated with poor HRM perceptions [16], and a meta-analysis of Ethiopian studies identified opportunities for professional growth as a strong correlate of job satisfaction [12].

text.text: Qualitative work in Ethiopian public hospitals describes centrally regulated staffing, salaries and employment arrangements that leave hospitals little room to tailor recruitment and development and that leave staff doubting management's ability to respond to workforce needs [10, 11].
text.formatted: Qualitative work in Ethiopian public hospitals describes centrally regulated staffing, salaries and employment arrangements that leave hospitals little room to tailor recruitment and development and that leave staff doubting management's ability to respond to workforce needs <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">11]</ref>.

text.text: Our finding that recruitment was among the least favorably rated domains fits this description.

The large between-hospital differences-from 1.5% favorable at the general hospital to 55.5% at Dilfana Primary Hospital-suggest that perceptions of HRM are partly a property of the organization rather than of the individual.

This is consistent with the notion of HRM system strength, in which the consistency and visibility of management practices shape shared employee perceptions [9], and with Ethiopian evidence that health worker motivation varies between hospitals [14].
text.formatted: This is consistent with the notion of HRM system strength, in which the consistency and visibility of management practices shape shared employee perceptions <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[9]</ref>, and with Ethiopian evidence that health worker motivation varies between hospitals <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[14]</ref>.

text.text: With only three hospitals, however, we cannot identify which hospital characteristics-size and patient load, leadership, staff composition or local implementation of national policies-explain these differences.
The persistence of the difference between Dilfana and Arba Minch General Hospital after adjustment indicates that it was not explained by the individual-level factors we measured.

The independent associations of recognition and autonomy with HRM perceptions are consistent with social exchange and organizational support theories, which predict that discretionary favorable treatment signals that the organization values its employees [19] [20] [21], and with job design research identifying autonomy as a core motivating job characteristic [33].

text.text: They also echo reviews and Ethiopian studies in which recognition and other nonfinancial HRM tools were among the most influential determinants of health worker motivation [4, 5, 13].

text.text: Alternative explanations must be considered.

Because all measures were self-reported at one time point, the associations may reflect reverse causation-staff who view HRM favorably may also report more recognition-or a general evaluative disposition that colors responses to all items.

Strengths of this study include random selection of hospitals and participants, a high response proportion, a theory-guided and pre-specified analysis, scales with good internal consistency, robust standard errors and extensive sensitivity analyses.
We also audited the data before analysis and report how duplicate and ineligible records were handled.
Limitations should also be considered.
First, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, and the direction of associations cannot be established.
Second, all variables were self-reported, so shared method variance and social desirability may have inflated associations.
Third, important covariates such as years of service, education, salary, employment status and department were not collected, so residual confounding is likely.

Finally, the study included three hospitals in one zone; hospital effects are confounded with unmeasured hospital characteristics, and the findings may not generalize to other regions, to referral hospitals or to primary health care facilities.
For hospital managers and zonal health departments, the findings suggest two practical priorities.

First, because perceptions differed so much between hospitals, hospital-level diagnosis of HRM practices-particularly recruitment, training and development, and performance appraisal-may be more useful than uniform zonal responses.
Second, recognition and decision latitude are non-financial resources that are at least partly within managers' control even under centrally regulated pay and staffing.

Whether strengthening them improves perceptions of HRM, and ultimately motivation, retention or quality of care, needs to be tested in longitudinal or intervention studies that use validated instruments, include more hospitals so that organizational factors can be modeled, and measure outcomes that matter for patients.

Fewer than one in three health professionals in public hospitals of Gamo Zone perceived HRM practices favorably, with recruitment and training and development rated least favorably and large differences between hospitals.
Perceived recognition and autonomy were independently associated with more favorable perceptions, whereas job demands were not after adjustment.

These cross-sectional associations identify hospital-level management and non-financial job resources as promising targets for further research and for efforts to strengthen health workforce governance in low-resource settings.
